items.title: Frank Chace Interview, 1961-11-18
items.q: I don't know exactly when or how often Pee-wee played in Chicago, but you can't discuss Chicago style without discussing Pee-wee's playing, I don't think.

ctx.x: Both you and I, I believe, feel that the Chicago School, as far as clarinet was concerned, was based on the inventions or the conceptions or the styles of the school. The styles of Teschmacher and Pee-wee-Pee-wee, not distinctly a Chicagoan, historically speaking, but yet so compatible with the Chicago style. Well, first of all, is that assumption correct, that they might have founded the elements of the Chicago style, as far as clarinet?

It's my assumption, yes. The actual historical business is vague to me. I don't know exactly when or how often Pee-wee played in Chicago, but you can't discuss Chicago style without discussing Pee-wee's playing, I don't think.
Do you remember any others of their general category? The early first generation horn men?

items.title: Frank Chace Interview, 1961-11-18
items.q: I asked him what he thought of Pee-wee Russell, and he demurred for a moment, and then he said, well, Pee-wee's a stylist.

ctx.x: The clarinetist who left Chicago and has joined those West Coast boys. Bob McCracken? McCracken, for one. I don't hear anything particularly derivative in Bob, nor anything particularly characteristic. Am I right about that? I think so.

When I was first learning how to play, I bought a clarinet from McCracken. I was very young, and I asked him what he thought of Pee-wee Russell, and he demurred for a moment, and then he said, well, Pee-wee's a stylist. And then either said nothing or talked about something else. McCracken, I guess, is, as far as I know, an extremely accomplished clarinet player, but my opinion is that there are thousands like that, and it's awfully hard to try to figure out what connection they have with traditional jazz. I…

They learned the tunes, and they may have shaped the tune a little in terms of what they heard somebody else play, but retained an indifference rather than developed a personality or developed a copy style.
